newsitem.title: USA: Cominco urges greater openness on LME.
newsitem.headline: Cominco urges greater openness on LME.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange should provide more detailed information on warehouse stock brands and ownership to tell the market if large positions were being built up, David Thompson, president and CEO of Cominco Ltd said.

Thompson, in a presentation at the annual American Zinc Association conference here, hoped the U.K. Securities and Investment Board's post-Sumitomo review of the LME will lead to greater provision of stock data, such as brands held, and true availability.
"Not all LME brands are acceptable to customers and considerable quantities of the LME stock are being held on long term warehouse rental contracts, so they are not available," Thompson said.
The market should be told if a player holds more than 10 percent of trading positions or stocks in warehouse, Thompson added.

"If the zinc industry had been aware in 1992 that at least one market player was building a major long position, then the industry might - just might - have adjusted its production of zinc," Thompson said, referring to Asturiana de Zinc.

In addtion, over the long term the LME's zinc contract, based on special high grade material, might become obsolescent as a pricing basis because production of galvanizing CGG slab and jumbos was rising.

In a later presentation, LME chief executive officer David King replied to Thompson's issue of one major player building the long position in the early 1990s. "In fact most of that activity was outside the reach of the LME and we were not aware of those positions ourselves," King said.

The LME has been looking at how the U.S. handles data about large positions. "The possibility we are considering is publishing, without naming the client by name, but just saying for example a certain client has a certain tonnage, long or short position, in the nearby months or whatever method used," King said.
"We are also considering saying that a certain entity held a certain percentage of stocks," King added. Daily publication of stock reports was also being looked at.

Regarding LME stocks, King said the exchange was looking at the issue of in and out charges at warehouses and incentives to keep metal locked up for long periods to see if such data "could be or should be published".
But King said it was difficult to obtain data on which stocks were tied up in long term storage deals, and what metal was immediately available.
The LME had no jurisdiction over users, non-members and banks who finance such deals, King said.
Stock brands and ownership issues were up for discussion now and King welcomed any industry comment and participation in the debate.
The LME also held recent talks with South Korean government officials about locating a warehouse there. Taiwan was also targetted.
